content: 1. In the post-validation phase, it is essential to explore and implement combination treatment regimens to ensure the sustainability of kala-azar elimination efforts. 2. Strengthening and maintaining the capacity of designated tertiary or secondary-level facilities for specialized diagnosis and treatment of kala-azar, post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), relapse cases, and HIV co-infections is critical in all endemic countries. 3. Referral systems, confirmatory diagnosis, and case management for kala-azar-HIV co-infections, relapse cases, and other complicated scenarios, such as kala-azar during pregnancy, must be reinforced at specialized tertiary facilities, including centers of excellence. 4. All kala-azar patients should be followed up and clinically reassessed for at least three years post-treatment to identify and manage the majority of PKDL cases (over 95%). Additionally, monitoring case fatality rates during the post-treatment follow-up period is necessary. 5. Collaboration with HIV programs is vital to ensure that all HIV patients in kala-azar-endemic areas are screened for kala-azar, and all kala-azar patients diagnosed at primary healthcare centers are tested for HIV. 6. Evidence must be generated and treatment guidelines updated for relapse cases, with dissemination of this information at all levels of the healthcare system. 7. Prevention, early management, and reporting of adverse drug events associated with kala-azar and PKDL treatments should be integrated into existing national pharmacovigilance programs. Reporting of serious adverse drug reactions must be made mandatory. 8. Addressing the lack of entomological capacity is a significant challenge for kala-azar elimination and the control of vector-borne diseases in the region. Strengthening entomological capacity in a cost-effective and sustainable manner is crucial. 9. As human cases decline, optimizing the efficiency and sustainability of vector control and surveillance through innovation and integration is increasingly necessary, particularly as ownership transitions from partners to governments. 10. Countries, with the support of research and implementation partners, must generate evidence to determine an exit strategy for entomological interventions and validate integrated vector surveillance and control approaches for kala-azar and other vector-borne diseases. 11. Vector control and surveillance must be mainstreamed into health system functions to ensure sustainability. Addressing socio-environmental determinants of kala-azar transmission, such as housing conditions in endemic communities, is essential to control transmission at its source. 12. Integrated vector management (IVM) approaches, which leverage lessons from integrated pest management in agriculture, are promoted by WHO. These approaches are well-suited for vector control and surveillance, as some vectors are responsible for multiple diseases, and certain interventions are effective against several vectors. 13. Training programs, such as the integrated field entomology training conducted in Nepal in July 2022, enhance the capacity for identifying, collecting, and controlling various vectors. These programs also facilitate the integration of entomological activities across multiple vector-borne diseases. 14. Geospatial mapping and modeling should be explored and operationalized to optimize case-based vector control as an exit strategy for kala-azar elimination. 15. Feasible and effective approaches to integrated vector surveillance and control for kala-azar and other vector-borne diseases should be validated and implemented in local settings. 16. Vector surveillance data should be utilized for overall vector control planning, and monitoring of impacts should be mandated. 17. Insecticide resistance monitoring must be institutionalized, strengthened, and sustained as part of the overall vector-borne disease program. 18. Integrated vector control working groups, represented by key stakeholders at national and state levels, should be established for systematic planning and monitoring of entomological interventions for all relevant vector-borne diseases, including kala-azar. 19. Collaboration with relevant authorities to improve housing and sanitation, including the use of screening, insecticide painting, and plastering, should be promoted as sustainable solutions for vector control. 20. National strategic plans for accelerating and sustaining kala-azar elimination should be developed or updated, with clear responsibilities and linkages between authorities and a focus on optimizing, integrating, and strengthening primary healthcare and health systems. 21. A national task force should be maintained at the central level to oversee elimination progress, coordinate with authorities and partners, and guide strategic actions. 22. Community awareness and engagement are critical for effective surveillance and vector control interventions. Regular social and community mobilization efforts are particularly important in the preand post-validation phases when case numbers decline, and general awareness of the disease diminishes. 23. Community outreach and health promotion activities for kala-azar and PKDL should be integrated with similar efforts for other diseases to enhance visibility, community acceptance, and cost-effectiveness. 24. Improved housing, nutrition, and targeted communication with impoverished communities are necessary to address the social determinants of kala-azar transmission and sustain the impacts of public health interventions. 25. High-level political commitment and resource allocation from countries and partners are essential to achieve and sustain kala-azar elimination, particularly in the final stages of disease elimination. 26. Regional partnerships involving member states, WHO, researchers, partners, and donors should advocate for high-level commitments and resource allocation, facilitate cross-border collaboration, and foster innovation to address programmatic gaps. 27. Mechanisms for cross-border surveillance and notification of kala-azar and PKDL should be established, with standardized reporting indicators and data-sharing systems across countries. 28. A regional and national network of health ministries, R&D partners, and donors should be established to share programmatic and knowledge gaps, mobilize resources, and accelerate innovation and research for kala-azar elimination. 29. Operational research and innovation priorities include tracking migration of kala-azar and PKDL cases, optimizing surveillance through geospatial mapping, and integrating vector surveillance and control for multiple diseases in local settings. 30. Cost-effective vector control tools and strategies, particularly for the post-validation phase, should be developed and implemented to ensure sustainability.
